content.p: Caylee Marie Anthony was two years old when she was last seen alive, on 16 June 2008, at her family's home in Orlando, Florida. Her mother, Casey Anthony, did not report her missing, and her grandmother did not call 911 until 15 July. Skeletal remains were found in woods near the family home that December. On 5 July 2011 a jury acquitted Casey Anthony on all three counts that tied her to Caylee's death: murder, manslaughter and child abuse. She was convicted only of four counts of giving false information to law enforcement, two of which an appeals court later threw out.

No one has been convicted of causing Caylee's death. The medical examiner could not say how she died, and the jury found the state had not proved its theory. Years later, the trial judge, Belvin Perry, said one question was still on everyone's mind: what really happened.

The case became public on 15 July 2008, when Caylee's grandmother, Cindy Anthony, called police. According to Oxygen's account of the call, she said: "I found out my granddaughter has been taken. She has been missing for a month." CNN counted 31 days since the child was last seen. Cindy's husband, George Anthony, testified at the trial that he had collected Casey's car from a tow yard that day and been concerned by a smell in the trunk that he compared to a human corpse. Later that day, he said, his wife called 911, and she told the dispatcher: "It smells like there's been a dead body in the damn car."

Casey Anthony, then 22, told police that she had left Caylee with a nanny named Zenaida Fernandez-Gonzalez, also called "Zanny". CNN reported that the story turned out to be made up, and that when police took Casey to Universal Studios, where she claimed to work, they learned she had lied about having a job there. She was arrested on 16 July on suspicion of child neglect, filing false official statements and obstructing an investigation. Those statements to Orange County detective Yuri Melich later became the basis of her four convictions.

She bonded out and was jailed again more than once. At the end of August 2008 the Orlando Sentinel reported that the bail-bond agency that had helped release her had rescinded its bond, a decision that bounty hunter Leonard Padilla, who had helped arrange her release, said was driven mainly by an angry crowd outside her parents' home, and that she had been arrested on charges of stealing and cashing checks belonging to a friend. On 5 September she walked out of the Orange County Jail for the second time in 15 days, after somebody whom authorities would not name posted a $500,000 bond. By then investigators were saying publicly that they had found traces of chloroform in her car and internet searches of chloroform websites on her computer, along with evidence of human decomposition in the trunk, CNN reported.

In October 2008 a grand jury indicted her on seven counts. Murder in the first degree was the gravest; the others were aggravated abuse, aggravated manslaughter, both involving the child, and four counts of providing false information to detectives. The state dropped the earlier child-neglect charge, saying in a statement that it had been "premised on the theory that her child, Caylee Marie, was still alive."

A utility meter reader, Roy Kronk, found the remains on 11 December 2008. He had already called authorities three times in August 2008 to say he had seen an object near the road that looked to him like a skull. Deputies found nothing then. Oxygen reported that he testified a deputy "berated me for a half hour for wasting his time". When he went back in December he used a stick to move the object, and he told the court he apologised for it: "I did not know what it was. I never lifted it off the ground."

The remains lay in a blanket inside a trash bag, in woods a short distance from the Anthony house. Police confirmed on 19 December that the remains were Caylee's, according to the Oxygen account citing ABC News. Dr. Jan Garavaglia, the medical examiner for Orange and Osceola counties, said in 2018 that three things made the death a homicide in her view: the lack of any credible explanation when the child was reported missing, the way the body had been hidden in bags and thrown behind a rotting log, and duct tape still present on the face. By the time the remains were found, they were too decomposed for the medical examiner to determine a cause of death, which was recorded as "homicide by undetermined means," ABC reported.
content.h2: Two accounts of one June day
content.p: The trial opened on 24 May 2011 before Chief Judge Belvin Perry. Because of local publicity, jurors were brought in from the Tampa Bay area and kept in a hotel for the whole trial. The Orlando Sentinel counted a 36-day trial with dozens of witnesses and hundreds of items of evidence. Casey Anthony did not testify.

Prosecutors told the jury that she suffocated Caylee with duct tape, and CNN reported that they also alleged chloroform. Their opening statement walked through each of the 31 days, using phone records and testimony from friends, lovers and family to show nightclub visits and two trips to a tattoo parlor, where she was tattooed with the words "Bella Vita", Italian for "beautiful life". Prosecutor Jeff Ashton told jurors in closing that Casey had decided on 16 June that "something had to be sacrificed", and that Caylee, then nearly three and beginning to talk, would not cooperate with her mother's lies. Lead prosecutor Linda Drane Burdick closed by asking whose life was better without Caylee.

The defence opened with a different account. Lawyer Jose Baez told jurors that Caylee drowned in the family's swimming pool on 16 June 2008. He said her father, George Anthony, found the body and helped dispose of it, and alleged that George had sexually abused Casey from childhood, which he said explained why she hid her pain and lied. George Anthony denied the accusations, and testified that opening statements were the first time he had heard of any drowning. Baez also suggested that Roy Kronk had moved the body, hoping to collect a reward, which Kronk denied under questioning. The prosecution called the cover-up claim absurd; Ashton told jurors that no one makes an accident look like a murder.

Neither side gave the jury firm proof. NBC News noted before closing arguments that the medical examiner never determined how Caylee died, and that Casey Anthony's DNA had not been found with the remains. The defence, it said, offered no evidence that she was molested or that the girl drowned. No physical evidence linked Casey to the traces of chloroform in the trunk, NBC added, and the state relied heavily on lies she told and on an odour in her car that its experts said was consistent with human decomposition. The air samples, produced by scientist Dr. Arpad Vass, were controversial. Baez dismissed the forensic case as "fantasy forensics" in closing and said of the cause of death: "The key question in this case will never be answered."
The summations grew so heated that Judge Perry stopped them and threatened to remove any lawyer who kept squabbling, saying that "orders or anything else may not mean a hill of a bean to any of you".

The jury of seven women and five men took less than 11 hours over two days. The clerk read the verdicts at 2:15 p.m. on Tuesday 5 July 2011: not guilty on the murder count, not guilty on the child-abuse count, not guilty on the manslaughter count, and guilty on four counts of lying to law enforcement. Anthony wept, then hugged Baez, and later mouthed "thank you" to him. Her parents left the courtroom without speaking to her.

"While we're happy for Casey, there are no winners in this case," Baez said afterward. Prosecutors looked stunned. State Attorney Lawson Lamar told reporters his team was "disappointed with the verdict today and surprised, because we know the facts", but that the system had worked. Defence lawyer Cheney Mason, speaking to reporters, said he hoped it was a lesson to those who had "indulged in media assassination".

Juror No. 3, Jennifer Ford, told ABC News that jurors were "sick to their stomach" about the decision. "I did not say she was innocent," she said. "I just said there was not enough evidence. If you cannot prove what the crime was, you cannot determine what the punishment should be." An alternate juror who did not take part in deliberations, Russell Huekler, said the prosecution had not shown motive or how Caylee died. Judge Perry signed an order barring the release of jurors' names, although Florida normally releases them. George, Cindy and Lee Anthony said in a statement that they believed the jury had made a fair decision, and that despite what they called the "baseless defense chosen by Casey Anthony" they would try to rebuild their lives privately.

Years later, Perry said in a CNN interview that he thought the state had proved its case and thought there was a high probability of a conviction for "some form of homicide". He noted that jurors had said they could not convict because the state could not prove how Caylee died. Separately, the Associated Press reported in 2017 that Florida's Department of Children and Families had concluded Anthony was responsible for her daughter's death, and that Perry had theorised she may have killed Caylee accidentally while using chloroform to calm her. That was an opinion, not a finding of any court.

On Thursday 7 July Perry sentenced Anthony to one year on each of the four counts, to run consecutively, and fined her $4,000. Because of credit for the time she had spent in jail, she was released from the Orange County Jail on Sunday 17 July 2011. CNN reported that she left shortly after midnight, and that about 1,000 people jeered as police guards and Baez escorted her to a waiting vehicle.

She also had to serve a year of probation from an earlier check fraud conviction in 2010, and Perry ordered her to repay more than $217,000 to four agencies for the search for Caylee. NBC reported that he raised the figure by $119,000 in September 2011 after the sheriff's office provided a more detailed breakdown, still short of the $500,000 prosecutors had sought, and that the order was a civil judgment, meaning creditors could pursue any income from a book deal or the rights to her story.

On 25 January 2013 Florida's Fifth District Court of Appeal threw out two of the four lying convictions on double-jeopardy grounds. It held that she could properly be convicted of two counts: she had given false information to Detective Melich during two separate interviews, hours apart. The court rejected her arguments that she was in custody without Miranda warnings and that the statute was unconstitutionally vague. ABC noted that the ruling would not affect her punishment, since she had already served her sentence and probation. Her lawyer Cheney Mason said she responded: "We keep fighting."

The criminal case left civil claims behind. Zenaida Gonzalez, a Florida woman who shares a name with the fictional nanny, sued Anthony for defamation in 2008, saying she lost her job and was evicted. In April 2012 a circuit judge ruled that a jury had to decide the disputed questions. In an October 2011 deposition, Anthony's lawyers invoked the Fifth Amendment 60 times, CNN reported, and her lawyer would not let her answer whether she had ever met Gonzalez. Anthony filed for bankruptcy in January 2013, listing about $1,000 in assets and $792,000 in liabilities, the Christian Science Monitor reported. The debts included about $500,000 in lawyers' fees and $145,660 for the Orange County Sheriff's Office. A federal bankruptcy judge, K. Rodney May, moved the Gonzalez case and one by Roy Kronk into bankruptcy court. In September 2015 Judge May dismissed Gonzalez's claim, concluding that Anthony's fabricated account "did not implicate Plaintiff in the disappearance of the child". ClickOrlando reported at that time that Kronk's suit remained open.

In 2017 Anthony gave the Associated Press her first interviews about the case. She said she still did not know what happened to her daughter: "I'm still not even certain as I stand here today about what happened." The AP said her responses were often contradictory. She admitted to the AP that she had lied to police, including about working at Universal Studios and about leaving Caylee with a babysitter.

In March 2025 Anthony, then 38, began posting on TikTok to promote herself as a "legal advocate", in a series that she started with a $10 monthly subscription. The lawyer who had represented her parents, Brad Conway, told Fox News she was using "her infamy" to get "attention and money", according to Local 10.
